section_summary: This section comprises U.S. State Department despatches, telegrams, cross-reference sheets, and research memoranda dating from May 1940 to January 1943 concerning religious affairs, church reorganization, and ideological policy in Japan and its empire. It details the Japanese government's enforcement of the Religious Bodies Law of 1939, which compelled the merger of Protestant denominations into the state-sanctioned Church of Christ in Japan, curtailed foreign missionary activities, and imposed strict administrative oversight on Roman Catholic, Protestant, and Orthodox bodies. In addition, memoranda by veteran missionaries and scholars, notably Boude C. Moore and M. Searle Bates, analyze the theological adaptation of State Shinto, Emperor veneration, and the official mobilization of religion in support of wartime nationalism and the 'New Order in East Asia.'

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Telegram No. 741 from Tokyo regarding Japanese military hostility toward foreign missionaries.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram 741 (August 24, 1940): Grew reports a military-instigated movement against foreign missionaries since early August; Bishop Heaslett thinks it ends their work.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Movement Against Foreign Missionaries in Japan

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting Japanese interest in Islam to counteract Soviet influence in Western China and Central Asia.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 154 from Tehran: Engert reports Japan encouraged study of Islam to use students in Western China against Soviet influence among Chinese Muslims, and sees Tehran and Kabul as posts for watching Soviet Central Asia.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 154 from Tehran Regarding Japanese Study and Strategic Use of Islam

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting the diplomatic sensation caused by the conversion of Japanese Legation Attaché Keiichi Kawasaki to Islam in Tehran.
subfiles.summary: Engert reports Tehran's sensation at attache Keiichi Kawasaki's conversion to Islam before Shariat Sangalaji, taking the name Abdollah; the Japanese Minister says it was sincere and voluntary.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1843: Conversion to Islam of a Member of the Japanese Legation

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Telegram No. 765 from Tokyo regarding the planned amalgamation of Christian denominations in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram 765 (August 30, 1940): fifty Christian representatives decided to merge Protestant sects to fit the new national structure; Catholics were absent.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Amalgamation of Christian Organizations in Japan

subfiles.about: Telegram detailing press accounts of Japanese Christian denominations uniting and eliminating foreign influence.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 765: fifty representatives under Bishop Abe resolve to conform to the new national structure, merge denominations and end foreign financial help and control, with talks on missions in Manchukuo and China planned.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 765 from Tokyo on Reorganization and Amalgamation of Christian Churches

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet quoting Despatch No. 654 from Yokohama on state supervision and the survival of Christian identity in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 654 (May 29, 1940): intensive government surveillance raises doubts whether Christianity can survive in Japan given the discrepancy with official ideology.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Official Japanese Supervision and Survival of Christianity

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet requesting an advisory opinion on classifying Nichiren Buddhist priests as ministers of religion under immigration law.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 654 (May 29, 1940): Boyce asks an opinion on classifying Nichiren priests as ministers of religion despite their political teachings.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Religious Classification of Nichiren Buddhist Priests

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting Telegram No. 868 regarding a public campaign and rally denouncing Christian churches in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Telegram 868 (September 20, 1940): an escalating movement against all Christian churches in Japan, with a mass denunciation meeting planned next day.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Public Movement Against Christian Churches in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet citing Despatch No. 5092 on integrating Japanese Christian churches into the totalitarian new structure.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Despatch 5092 (October 28, 1940): the movement to unite Christian churches in Japan into the totalitarian new structure, filed at 394.0063/9.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Union of Christian Churches under Totalitarian New Structure

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting visa applications by nine Japanese Christian leaders traveling to the U.S. for peace discussions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a March 11, 1941 telegram: nine Japanese Christian leaders plan to seek U.S. visitor visas to consult on preserving peace.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Visa Applications of Japanese Christian Leaders for Peace Mission

subfiles.about: Detailed report on the historical background, organization, eleven temporary branches, and creed of the newly formed Church of Christ in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This report outlines the formation of the Church of Christ in Japan (Nippon Kirisuto Kyodan) as a milestone in ecumenical and Japanese church history. It examines earlier union initiatives, the administrative impact of the 1939 Religious Bodies Law, and the domestic structural crisis of 1940 that culminated in the October mass meeting endorsing unification. The document describes the church's organizational framework, which temporarily grouped existing denominations into eleven numbered branches under an elected head, while establishing the Apostles' Creed and Scripture as its doctrinal foundation.
subfiles.title: The Church of Christ in Japan

subfiles.about: Missionary circular letters reporting on state pressure on churches in Japan and personal family news from Washington, D.C.
subfiles.from: S. M. Erickson and Lois J. Erickson
subfiles.summary: Rev. S. M. Erickson describes Japan's Religions Control Law, Protestant amalgamation, Mitsuru Tomita's selection and missionaries' precarious position; Lois Erickson gives Washington activities and family news; both love Japan and pray for an end to military control.
subfiles.title: Circular Letters to Friends Regarding the Christian Movement in Japan and Family News

subfiles.about: Memorandum recording missionary Boude C. Moore's observations on theological innovation and the political power of Shinto in wartime Japan.
subfiles.summary: Laurence E. Salisbury transmits and records detailed statements by veteran missionary Boude C. Moore regarding recent theological developments in Shinto. Moore, who attended Shinto courses at Tokyo Imperial University, explains that Shinto theologians incorporated Christian concepts of a single absolute creator (Zettai no Kami) and purification as absolution to compensate for perceived doctrinal deficiencies. The memorandum highlights the pervasive identification of the Emperor and the Japanese race with the divine spirit, the inherently religious nature of state shrines as expounded by Dr. Genchi Kato, and Shinto's deep institutional stability compared to modern Western political ideologies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Laurence E. Salisbury on Statements by Boude C. Moore Regarding Recent Developments in the Shinto Religion

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet noting a Keijo consular despatch transmitting Professor Chikao Fujisawa's pamphlet on Shinto purification rituals.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grew aboard the Gripsholm transmits Consul Quarton's despatch on Chikao Fujisawa's pamphlet on the Shinto purification ritual, filed at 894.00/1160.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Despatch on Chikao Fujisawa's Pamphlet on Shinto Purification Ritual

subfiles.about: Diplomatic report from Vatican City describing the subjugation and official pressures facing Christian denominations in Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Tittmann relays Vatican information: French and German vicars in Korea forced out or replaced, foreign clergy in Japan face confiscation, arrest and segregation, pressure to add imperial rites to Catholic liturgy, and growing docility among Protestants and Orthodox.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 25: Situation of Roman Catholic and Other Religions in Japan

subfiles.about: Instruction transmitting a Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing the final consolidation of Japanese Protestant denominations into a single church.
subfiles.summary: Instruction 190 sends Chungking Benninghoff's December 23, 1942 memorandum on the Church of Christ in Japan's full Protestant amalgamation, the Education Ministry's Religions Bureau pressure, and fears censorship will de-Christianize it.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 190 to Chungking Transmitting Memorandum on The Church of Christ in Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing H. J. Timperley's letter transmitting Dr. M. S. Bates's memorandum on Church-State problems in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to H. J. Timperley's January 16, 1943 letter enclosing M. S. Bates's memorandum on church and state in the Far East, filed at 894.404/38.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference File Note: Dr. M. S. Bates's Memorandum on Problems of State and Church in the Far East

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing Dr. M. S. Bates's study on Church-State relations in China, Japan, Taiwan, and Korea.
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Bates: religious freedom largely safe in Free China, unlike State Shinto's totalitarian loyalty in Japan; the Education Rescript's indoctrination, Japanese Christians' theological confusion, and assimilation in Taiwan, Korea and occupied China.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Laurence E. Salisbury Summarizing Dr. M. S. Bates's Memorandum 'Materials on Problems of State and Church in the Far East'

subfiles.about: Transmittal letter and first sections of Dr. M. S. Bates's monograph on Church-State relations, State Shinto, and wartime pressures on Christianity in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: H. J. Timperley forwards to George Atcheson a copy of Dr. M. S. Bates's study analyzing Church and State relations in East Asia. The text surveys religious liberty and educational policy in Free China, where Christianity enjoys public respect, before providing an exhaustive examination of Japan's totalitarian state apparatus and State Shinto. Bates details compulsory shrine veneration, ethical indoctrination through the Imperial Rescript on Education, the enactment of the Religious Bodies Law of 1939, and the profound ideological compromises made by Japanese Christian leaders attempting to align their faith with imperial war aims.
subfiles.title: Letter from H. J. Timperley Transmitting Memorandum by Dr. M. S. Bates, 'Materials on Problems of State and Church in the Far East'
